descriptor: Gulf Coast wetlands: human activities that change sediment delivery, harm from sediment loss, effects of Mississippi fertilizer runoff on the Gulf, economic costs, and a non-fertilizer-reduction way to cut nutrient flow.
solution:
(a) Two activities, each with its mechanism. Levees and channelization confine the river so sediment is shot out to deep water instead of spreading over the delta; dams and reservoirs trap sediment upstream, so less travels downstream; dredged canals and navigation channels divert flow and let seawater in. *(1 point per activity named, 1 per correct explanation of the effect on sediment flow; 4 points.)*

(b) Two harms. Without fresh sediment the marsh surface cannot build up as the land sinks, so wetlands drown and convert to open water; the lost marsh and barrier land no longer buffers storm surge, and nursery habitat for fish, shrimp and birds shrinks, lowering biodiversity and productivity. *(2 points.)*

(c)(i) Two impacts of fertilizer reaching the Gulf: nitrogen and phosphorus drive algal blooms; when the algae die, decomposers use up dissolved oxygen, producing a hypoxic "dead zone" where fish and shellfish die or flee; reduced light penetration also damages seagrass. *(2 points.)*
(ii) Two economic consequences: lower commercial and recreational fishing catches (lost income, jobs); reduced tourism and higher costs for water treatment or monitoring. *(2 points.)*
(iii) Another strategy: restore or build wetlands and vegetated buffer strips that trap nutrients before they enter the river, or upgrade wastewater treatment to remove nutrients. *(1 point.)*

descriptor: Compares battery electric and gasoline vehicles: government incentives, fuel cost per mile for each, charging cost from a 4.0 kW charger over 7.0 h, difference in CO2 per 100 miles, and economic effects of more BEVs.
solution:
(a) Three federal strategies: tax credits or rebates for buying BEVs; funding or mandating public charging stations; higher fuel taxes on gasoline (also: subsidies for manufacturers, fleet purchase requirements, public education). *(3 points.)*

(b) Gasoline cost per mile = price ÷ efficiency = $3.75/gal ÷ 25 mi/gal = **$0.15 per mile**. *(1 point setup with units, 1 point answer.)*

(c)(i) Energy = power × time = 4.0 kW × 7.0 h = 28 kWh; cost = 28 kWh × $0.11/kWh = **$3.08**. *(setup, answer.)*
(c)(ii) $3.08 ÷ 100 mi = **$0.031 per mile** (about 3 cents), roughly one fifth of the gasoline cost. *(1 point.)*

(d) ICE total = 72.8 + 17.7 = 90.5 lb CO2; BEV total = 63.6 lb (all upstream, from coal-fired electricity). Difference = 90.5 − 63.6 = **26.9 lb CO2 less for the BEV** per 100 miles. *(1 point.)*

(e) Two economic impacts: higher demand for electricity may raise power prices or require new generating capacity and grid upgrades; charging infrastructure creates jobs and investment, while gasoline stations, refiners and repair shops lose business and revenue. Highway fuel-tax revenue also falls. *(2 points; exclude climate costs and pump price.)*

descriptor: Ozone in two atmospheric layers: UV absorbed by the stratospheric layer and a health benefit, the formation/breakdown balance, CFC destruction chemistry and why recovery is slow, tropospheric ozone formation and its impacts.
solution:
(a) Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet (mainly UV-B and UV-C) radiation; the health benefit is lower rates of skin cancer, sunburn or cataracts. *(1 + 1.)*

(b) UV splits ozone: O₃ + UV → O₂ + O. The free oxygen atom meets an O₂ molecule: O + O₂ → O₃. The two steps continuously recycle ozone and absorb UV. *(1 point for each process.)*

(c)(i) UV breaks chlorine atoms off CFC molecules (e.g., CCl₃F + UV → CCl₂F + Cl); each free Cl then attacks ozone: Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂, and the chlorine is regenerated so one atom destroys many ozone molecules. *(1 + 1.)*
(ii) Ozone recovery lags because CFCs are very long-lived and take years to reach the stratosphere, chlorine already present stays aloft for decades, and other ozone-depleting substances are still emitted. *(1 point for one.)*

(d) Burning fossil fuels (e.g., vehicle exhaust) emits NOₓ and VOCs, which react to form ozone. Ozone peaks in the daytime because the reactions are photochemical and need sunlight. *(1 + 1.)*

(e) Ecological: ozone damages plant tissue and reduces photosynthesis/crop growth. Health: ozone irritates the respiratory system and aggravates asthma. *(1 + 1.)*

descriptor: Biodiversity: two traits of high-biodiversity ecosystems, two human activities that reduce it with mechanisms, practical solutions for each, one natural cause of loss, and two ecological benefits.
solution:
(a) Two shared traits: many different species with large numbers of individuals each, complex food webs and many niches, high genetic variation. *(2 points.)*

(b) Two activities with mechanisms: clearing land for development or logging removes and fragments habitat; introducing invasive species lets them outcompete natives; monoculture agriculture replaces diverse natives; fertilizer or sewage runoff lowers dissolved oxygen so only tolerant species persist; overharvesting removes keystone species or top predators. *(1 per activity, 1 per mechanism; 4 points.)*

(c) A practical solution for each, linked: cluster development or smart growth and wildlife corridors for development; selective cutting and replanting for logging; border inspections and public education for invasives; buffer strips or advanced sewage treatment for runoff; quotas and enforcement for harvest. *(1 each; 2 points.)*

(d) One natural factor: volcanic eruption or asteroid impact darkening the sky, wildfire, drought, hurricane damage to coastal nurseries, or a new disease. *(1 point.)*

(e) Two benefits: greater resilience and stability of the ecosystem; pollination and pest control; natural water and air purification; more genetic material for adaptation; faster nutrient cycling by soil organisms. *(2 points.)*

descriptor: Nuclear plant proposal for a river town: judge two claims (solid waste, greenhouse gases), construction-phase environmental problems, normal-operation pollutant, its ecological effect and control system, electricity-saving steps, and an accident example.
solution:
(a)(i) Disagree: spent fuel rods and contaminated tools and clothing are radioactive wastes that must be isolated for very long periods. *(1.)* (ii) Either position can be defended if justified: agree because no fossil fuel is burned in operation; disagree because mining, enrichment, transport and construction use fossil energy, and cooling releases water vapor. *(1.)*

(b) Two construction problems: clearing and fragmenting riparian habitat, soil compaction, erosion and sediment runoff, noise and exhaust from machinery, construction waste. *(2.)*

(c)(i) The most likely river pollutant in normal operation is thermal pollution from heated cooling water (not radioactive release). *(1.)*
(ii) Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen and raises metabolic rates, causing thermal shock or fish kills and shifting community composition. *(1.)*
(iii) Cooling towers, cooling ponds or canals let the water shed heat before discharge. *(1.)*

(d) Two steps: replace old appliances and bulbs with efficient ones (LEDs); raise insulation or adjust thermostats; turn off or unplug idle devices. *(2.)*

(e) Accidents: Three Mile Island, Chernobyl or Fukushima Daiichi. One consequence: radioactive contamination spreading through food webs, killing plants and animals or causing mutations and loss of biodiversity. *(1 + 1.)*

descriptor: Combined sewer overflow: two runoff pollutants, runoff volume from a 200 by 100 m parking lot and from 20 percent impervious city area after 5 cm rain, bypass volume at the plant, ways to cut runoff, a paving problem.
solution:
(a) Two pollutants: nitrogen or phosphorus (fertilizer), sediment, pathogens such as E. coli, motor oil, road salt, pesticides, trash. *(2.)*

(b) Area = 200 m × 100 m = 20,000 m²; depth 5 cm = 0.05 m. Volume = 20,000 m² × 0.05 m = **1,000 m³**. *(1 setup, 1 answer.)*

(c) City area 10 km² = 10 × 10⁶ m² = 1.0 × 10⁷ m²; impervious = 0.20 × 1.0 × 10⁷ = 2.0 × 10⁶ m². Runoff = 2.0 × 10⁶ m² × 0.05 m = **1.0 × 10⁵ m³** (100,000 m³). *(1 + 1.)*

(d) Flow arriving = 100,000 + 5,000 (domestic) = 105,000 m³; plant capacity 10,000 m³ per day. Bypass = 105,000 − 10,000 = **95,000 m³ untreated**. *(1.)*

(e) Reduce runoff by: replacing pavement with permeable surfaces or planting vegetation; building retention basins, wetlands, rain barrels or green roofs. *(2.)*

(f) Extensive pavement causes habitat loss and fragmentation, an urban heat island effect, or reduced aquifer recharge. *(1.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Rubric totals 10; (d) answer 95,000 m3 verified against guideline page image.

descriptor: Pacific Ring of Fire: what happens at subduction zones and why volcanoes form, primary succession and soil formation on new volcanic ground, tsunami generation and ecological harm, and transform-boundary behavior during and between earthquakes.
solution:
(a)(i) At a subduction zone, denser oceanic plate is forced beneath the other plate, often forming a deep trench. *(1.)*
(ii) The sinking slab heats and releases water, melting overlying mantle; the buoyant magma rises through the crust and erupts, building volcanic arcs and island chains. *(1 for melting, 1 for rising magma.)*

(b)(i) Primary succession is colonization of bare rock, ash or sand where no soil previously existed. *(1.)*
(ii) Pioneers such as lichens and mosses secrete acids and wedge into rock, weathering it into mineral particles; as they die and decompose, organic matter mixes with these particles, forming a thin soil that later plants can use. *(1 + 1.)*

(c)(i) A sudden vertical slip of the seafloor during a subduction earthquake displaces a huge volume of water, which radiates outward as waves growing taller in shallow water. *(1 + 1.)*
(ii) Tsunamis destroy coastal habitats (mangroves, reefs), drown land organisms, or contaminate soils with salt water. *(1.)*

(d)(i) At the moment of an earthquake, locked plates suddenly slip past each other horizontally, releasing stored energy. *(1.)*
(ii) Between quakes the plates stay stuck by friction while stress and strain accumulate. *(1.)*

descriptor: Carbon and phosphorus cycles: biological removal and return of atmospheric carbon, ocean sinks, a long-term land sink, other human carbon sources, a CO2-related problem with a consequence, and how phosphorus differs and why it is needed.
solution:
(a)(i) Photosynthesis: autotrophs take in CO₂ and build it into sugars and other organic molecules. *(1.)* (ii) Cellular respiration or decomposition converts organic carbon back to CO₂ (or CH₄ under anaerobic conditions) released to the air. *(1.)*

(b)(i) Two ocean sinks: CO₂ dissolves in seawater, where it forms carbonic acid and bicarbonate; marine organisms use carbon for shells and skeletons (calcium carbonate) that sink and become limestone; phytoplankton fix carbon and it sinks. *(2.)*
(ii) A long-term land sink: peat or wetland sediments, old-growth wood, soil organic matter, or carbonate rock. *(1.)*

(c) Other human activities: deforestation and burning biomass (removes sink and releases carbon); cement production, landfills and livestock produce CO₂ or methane. *(2.)*

(d) Problem: enhanced greenhouse effect causing global warming; consequence: sea-level rise and habitat loss, shifting climate zones, or ocean acidification dissolving shells. *(1 + 1.)*

(e)(i) Phosphorus has no significant atmospheric phase; it cycles slowly through rock, soil and water and is released by weathering. *(1.)* (ii) Needed for DNA, RNA, ATP and cell-membrane phospholipids (also bones and teeth). *(1.)*
notes: Rubric parts sum to more than 10; the printed exam maximum is 10 points. Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Rubric sums to 11; capped at 10.

descriptor: Everglades restoration: two human activities reducing freshwater inflow, phosphorus sources, effects and reduction, one climate-change impact each on water quantity, quality and habitat, and ecological and economic restoration benefits.
solution:
(a) Two activities that reduce inflow: diverting water for irrigation or flood-control canals; withdrawals for homes, industry and lawns; roads and filled wetlands that block sheet flow. *(2; must be described, not just named.)*

(b)(i) Phosphorus source: fertilizer runoff from farms or lawns, septic seepage, or discharge from plants lacking advanced treatment. *(1.)*
(ii) Excess phosphorus triggers algal blooms and eutrophication, or favors invasive cattails over native sawgrass adapted to low-nutrient water. *(1.)*
(iii) Link the fix to the source: buffer strips and constructed treatment wetlands for farm runoff, precision fertilizer use, or tertiary treatment. *(1.)*

(c) One example for each: water quantity: higher evaporation or sea-level rise lowers freshwater levels (or heavy storms increase flooding); water quality: warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, or saltwater intrusion raises salinity; habitat: saltwater pushes mangroves inland, displacing freshwater communities. *(3.)*

(d)(i) Restoring flow and water quality re-establishes native vegetation and habitat, stabilizing food webs and reducing algal blooms. *(1.)* (ii) Restoration increases tourism and recreation revenue and jobs, and avoids water-treatment costs. *(1.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Article stimulus not visible in extracted text. Rubric totals 10.

descriptor: Oil spills: read the high-estimate Deepwater Horizon volume from a bar graph, coastal environmental and economic impacts, dispersant pros and cons, a cleanup method, another oil source, and a petroleum substitute in a product.
solution:
(a) On the bar chart the highest estimate for the Deepwater Horizon (Gulf of Mexico, 2010) is just below 200 million gallons, accepted as any value from 185 to 199 million gallons. *(1 point with units.)*

(b) Two problems: oil coats birds and mammals, destroying insulation and buoyancy; smothered or poisoned marsh, beach and reef habitat disrupts food webs and loses nursery grounds; oil blocks light for photosynthesis. *(2.)*

(c) One economic impact: lost fishing and tourism income, or cleanup costs (a positive: temporary cleanup jobs). *(1.)*

(d)(i) Advantage: breaks slicks into droplets that dilute and disperse, protecting birds and shorelines. Disadvantage: dispersed oil and the chemicals can be toxic to marine life and the oil is not removed, harming the water column and seafloor. *(1 + 1.)*
(ii) Physical: floating booms and skimmers contain and collect surface oil; or biological: adding oil-degrading microbes. *(1.)*

(e) Other source: leaking boat engines and bilge discharge, stormwater runoff carrying oil from roads and cars, natural seeps, or leaks in drilling and pipelines; give how it reaches the water. *(1 + 1.)*

(f) Substitute: plant-derived plastic (corn-based bottles), paper bags, or cotton and hemp fibers in place of synthetic fabrics. *(1.)*

descriptor: Urban sprawl: causes, health effects, describe the trend between population density and petroleum use on a graph, smart-growth measures, ways to reduce harm to wildlife from roads and sprawl, and urban food production.
solution:
(a) Two causes: heavy reliance on cars and new highways; cheaper land and larger lots outside cities; higher inner-city taxes or poor schools and crime; telecommuting. *(2.)*

(b) Two health effects: respiratory disease from traffic pollution; obesity and hypertension from inactive car-based living; crash injuries; longer emergency response times. *(2.)*

(c) The graph shows an inverse (negative) relationship: cities with lower population density use more petroleum per person, and use falls as density rises. *(1.)*

(d) Two smart-growth steps: invest in mass transit and bike paths; mixed-use zoning and urban growth boundaries; tax incentives for infill and brownfield redevelopment. *(2.)*

(e) Two wildlife measures: wildlife overpasses or underpasses and corridors linking habitat; fencing along migration routes, preserved green buffers, or routing highways away from prime habitat. *(2.)*

(f) Urban food production: rooftop or community gardens, vertical farms or hydroponics, converting vacant lots. *(1.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Graph rendered and checked: per-capita petroleum use falls steeply as density rises (inverse curve). Rubric totals 10.

descriptor: White-nose syndrome in little brown bats: why disease rarely drives extinction, threats to tiny populations, slow recovery biology, effects of bat decline on other organisms, forest ecosystem services, and a reason emerging human diseases are rising.
solution:
(a) One reason: genetic variation means some individuals resist the pathogen and reproduce; or deaths reduce host density so transmission slows; or pathogens that kill every host lose their own habitat. *(1.)*

(b)(i) Two threats to a very small population: trouble finding mates; loss of genetic diversity (inbreeding, one disease or change affecting all); competition from similar species; reduced group protection, such as shared roost warmth. *(2.)*
(ii) Bats reproduce slowly (often one pup a year), mature late and have long generation times, so numbers rebound slowly. *(1.)*

(c) Two effects: insect prey increase (more crop pests and disease vectors); plants relying on bat pollination or seed dispersal decline; predators of bats lose food; guano-dependent cave communities shrink. *(2.)*

(d) Two forest services with human benefits: timber and fuel; carbon storage that slows climate change; soil protection and flood control; water purification; recreation and tourism. *(1 + 1 each pair.)*

(e) A likely reason: growing contact with wildlife through habitat clearing or wildlife trade spreads zoonotic disease to people; or increased global travel and dense populations spread pathogens quickly; or climate change widens vector ranges. *(1 for reason, 1 for explanation.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. The Fremont New Tribune article (image) is not visible in extracted text. Rubric totals 10.

descriptor: Iron and steel supply chain: calculate rock waste, pig iron from all reserves, ore reserve used for steel, coal saved by recycling, then abandoned mine problems, a mitigation method, and why surface mining costs less.
solution:
(a)(i) Waste = ore in − pig iron out = 1.6 − 1.2 = 0.4 billion tons = **4 × 10⁸ tons**. *(1.)*
(ii) Pig iron per ton of ore = 1.2 ÷ 1.6 = 0.75; applied to reserves: 0.75 × 800 billion = **600 billion tons**. *(1 setup, 1 answer.)*
(iii) Steel uses 95% of mined ore: 0.95 × 800 billion = **760 billion tons**. *(1.)*

(b) Coal saved = 0.7 tons coal/ton steel × 80 million tons recycled = **56 million tons per year**. *(1.)*

(c) Two problems at abandoned coal mines: acid mine drainage and heavy-metal runoff polluting streams; subsidence and sinkholes; habitat destruction and erosion; underground fires or methane release. *(2.)*

(d) One mitigation: neutralize acid drainage with limestone or retention ponds, replant and regrade slopes to stop erosion, or seal and fence shafts. *(1.)*

(e) Surface mining is cheaper because it needs fewer workers and less costly equipment and ventilation and has lower safety, insurance and legal liabilities than deep mining. *(2: reason plus discussion.)*

descriptor: US municipal solid waste graph: cause of a change in per-person waste 2000-2012, percent rise in total MSW 1980 to 2012, incineration and landfill drawbacks, landfill-gas power steps, tire pile health risk, composting benefit and drawback.
solution:
(a)(i) One cause: more reduction, reuse and recycling; lighter packaging; economic recession lowering consumption; digital media replacing paper. *(1.)*
(ii) From the graph, total MSW rose from about 150 to about 250 million tons: (250 − 150) ÷ 150 × 100 = **≈ 67%** (accepted 66% to 67%). *(1.)*

(b)(i) Incineration: releases air pollutants (particulates, dioxins, CO₂, NOₓ), leaves toxic ash, expensive to build. *(1.)* (ii) Landfills: leachate can contaminate groundwater, methane and odors escape, land is lost for other uses. *(1.)*

(c) Landfill gas electricity: (1) collect the methane produced by decomposing waste through wells and pipes; (2) burn the methane, converting chemical energy to heat that produces steam or drives an engine; (3) the steam or exhaust spins a turbine connected to a generator, making electricity. *(3.)*

(d) Tire piles collect rainwater that breeds mosquitoes that carry disease, and tire fires release toxic smoke harming respiration. *(1.)*

(e)(i) Compost provides a free soil amendment/fertilizer and can create jobs. *(1.)* (ii) Compost can attract pests, smell bad, or release methane if poorly managed; it requires labor and space. *(1.)*

descriptor: Soil: how two climate factors affect formation rate, biotic and abiotic components of the A horizon, nitrate groundwater pollution from agriculture, acid deposition effect on plants and remediation, and two climate-related soil degradation routes.
solution:
(a) Two climate factors: warmer temperatures and moderate rainfall speed weathering and decomposition, so soil forms faster; cold or dry conditions slow them (freeze-thaw can crack rock, but heavy rain also increases erosion, lowering soil accumulation); wind can add or strip particles. *(2.)*

(b) The A horizon (topsoil) is rich in humus. Biotic: earthworms, fungi, bacteria or roots. Abiotic: sand, silt, clay, minerals, air or water. *(1 + 1.)*

(c)(i) Practice: applying nitrogen fertilizer, or poorly built animal-waste lagoons. *(1.)* (ii) Nitrate is highly soluble and, not taken up by crops, percolates down through the soil to the aquifer (or enters surface water that recharges it). *(1.)*

(d)(i) Acid deposition lowers soil pH, leaching nutrient cations such as calcium and magnesium and mobilizing toxic aluminum, which damage roots and reduce growth. *(1.)* (ii) Spread lime (crushed limestone) to neutralize acidity. *(1.)*

(e) Two ways: warming and drought speed desertification and soil drying; faster decomposition lowers organic matter; heavy storms increase erosion; sea-level rise salinizes coastal soils. *(2.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Rubric totals 10.

descriptor: Microbeads and nutrients in wastewater: effects of ingested microbeads, how nitrates degrade water quality, primary-treatment plastic removal, a disinfection method, sludge on farmland pros and cons, and mangrove loss and services.
solution:
(a) Two effects: beads clog or fill the digestive tract so animals feel full and starve; beads carry toxic chemicals that accumulate in tissues and may magnify up the food chain. *(2.)*

(b) Nitrates fertilize algae, causing blooms (cultural eutrophication); when the algae die, decomposition by microbes consumes dissolved oxygen, creating hypoxic water that kills fish; blooms also cloud water and block light. *(1 for response, 1 for effect linked to it.)*

(c)(i) Primary treatment removes large plastic by screens or bar racks, settling tanks and skimmers. *(1.)* (ii) Disinfect with chlorine, ultraviolet light or ozone. *(1.)*
(iii) Advantage: biosolids are a nutrient-rich, low-cost fertilizer and avoid landfilling; disadvantage: they may contain heavy metals, pathogens or drug residues that contaminate soil and water, and may smell. *(1 + 1.)*

(d)(i) Mangroves are cut for shrimp farms, coastal development, agriculture, or wood and charcoal. *(1.)* (ii) Intact mangroves protect shorelines from storms and erosion and provide nursery habitat for fisheries. *(1.)*

descriptor: Haiti: reason for deforestation and a strategy to reduce it, how deforestation alters stream water quality, other forest benefits, then a fertility and life-expectancy data table and factors that could explain falling fertility and rising life expectancy.
solution:
(a)(i) Reason: forests are cleared for farmland, fuelwood or charcoal income, and enforcement is weaker. *(1.)* (ii) Strategy: enforce logging limits, promote efficient stoves or alternative fuels, sustainable forestry, or ecotourism. *(1.)*

(b) Change: warmer, more turbid stream water. Without canopy shade, sunlight warms the water; without roots and litter, soil erodes and washes in. (Alternatives: lower dissolved oxygen, more nutrient runoff.) *(1 + 1.)*

(e) A factor lowering fertility: more education and job opportunities for women, delaying marriage and births and increasing awareness of family planning; with lower infant mortality parents expect children to survive. *(1 + 1.)*

descriptor: Dams: how a hydroelectric dam generates electricity, two economic benefits besides power and flood control, ecological value of floodplain flooding, benefits and drawbacks of dam removal, and beaver dams as a keystone species.
solution:
(a) Water stored behind the dam has gravitational potential energy; released through intakes it falls and converts to kinetic energy, rotating turbine blades (mechanical energy); the turbine shaft spins a generator that converts the mechanical energy to electricity. *(3: one per step.)*

(b) Two benefits: recreation and tourism; reservoir water for irrigation, drinking and industry; jobs; fisheries or shipping. *(2.)*

(c) Seasonal floods deposit nutrient-rich sediment, recharge groundwater and maintain wetland and riparian habitat for fish and birds. *(1.)*

(d)(i) Removal reopens migration routes to spawning habitat and restores natural temperature and flow. *(1.)* (ii) Negatives: stored sediment and pollutants are released downstream, bank erosion, or loss of the lake habitat that has developed. *(1.)*

(e)(i) A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance. *(1.)* (ii) Beaver dams create ponds and wetlands, trap sediment, slow flow and reduce erosion, giving habitat to many other species. *(1.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Rubric totals 10.

descriptor: School renovation article: define carbon footprint, link a heating system to it and reduce it, two green-roof benefits, cafeteria practices, native-plant landscaping, and an environmental benefit of plant-based flooring over synthetic carpet.
solution:
(a)(i) A carbon footprint is the total carbon dioxide (and other carbon compounds) released by an activity, product or person. *(1.)* (ii) Burning fossil fuel (oil, natural gas) in boilers emits CO₂ (CO if combustion is incomplete). *(1.)* (iii) Add insulation or sealing, lower the thermostat schedule, or switch to a renewable or more efficient heat source. *(1.)*

(b) Two green-roof benefits: insulation that cuts heating and cooling energy; stormwater absorption; habitat for pollinators; reduced urban heat island; CO₂ uptake. *(2.)*

(c) Two cafeteria practices: composting scraps, donating surplus food, using reusable trays, offering more plant-based or local food (lower transport and meat impact), bulk packaging. *(2.)*

(d) Two native-plant benefits: adapted to local conditions, so they need less water, fertilizer and pesticide (saving money); they support native food webs and biodiversity and crowd out invasives. *(2.)*

(e) Cork or bamboo flooring is a renewable, biodegradable product made with fewer fossil fuels and fewer VOC emissions than synthetic carpet, and the growing plants store carbon. *(1.)*

descriptor: Offshore wind farm: environmental benefit, an economic effect, another ocean energy source, then calculations for 200 turbines of 4 MW and 2.0 million MWh annual demand: 80 percent of demand, revenue at $0.20 per kWh, and operating hours needed.
solution:
(a) Benefit: displaces fossil fuel generation, reducing CO₂ and air pollutants and fuel extraction damage; turbine bases can act as artificial reefs. *(1.)*

(b) Identify and describe one effect: job creation in construction and maintenance (positive), or reduced tourism and property values or high construction costs (negative). *(1 identify, 1 describe.)*

(c) Another ocean energy: tidal turbines, wave energy converters, or ocean thermal energy conversion. *(1.)*

(d) 0.80 × 2.0 × 10⁶ MWh = **1.6 × 10⁶ MWh**. *(1 + 1.)*

(e) Revenue = 1.6 × 10⁶ MWh × 1,000 kWh/MWh × $0.20/kWh = 1.6 × 10⁹ kWh × $0.20 = **$3.2 × 10⁸** ($320 million). *(1 + 1.)*

(f) Total capacity = 200 turbines × 4 MW = 800 MW; hours = 1.6 × 10⁶ MWh ÷ 800 MW = **2,000 hours**. *(1 + 1.)*

descriptor: Arctic food web diagram: name a producer, primary consumer and secondary consumer, what arrows mean, effects of less sea ice on polar bear hunting, the albedo feedback, and migration reasons plus a commercial threat and fix for right whales.
solution:
(a) Producer: diatom (phytoplankton); primary consumer: krill (zooplankton); secondary consumer: cod or seal (as drawn). *(3.)*

(b) The arrows also show the direction of energy (and matter) flow between trophic levels. *(1.)*

(c) With less ice there are fewer platforms and seal breathing holes, so bears must swim farther, expend more energy and wait longer between kills. *(1.)*

(d) Melting sea ice lowers surface albedo; dark open water absorbs more solar energy and warms, which melts more ice: a positive feedback that amplifies warming. *(1 for reduced reflectivity and more absorption, 1 for completing the loop.)*

(e)(i) Reasons to migrate: follow food, seek a milder climate, or reach breeding grounds. *(1.)*
(ii) Commercial activity: shipping lanes cause ship strikes; fishing gear entangles whales; seismic surveys and engines create disruptive noise. *(1.)*
(iii) Linked strategy: slow-speed zones and rerouting ships; modified or weak-link fishing gear; limits on seismic surveys or quieter engines. *(1.)*
notes: Exam form (US/Intl) is not stated in the source pages. Food-web figure not reproduced; organisms taken from the guideline. Rubric totals 10.

descriptor: Household biomass burning: two indoor pollutants and a respiratory illness, a realistic approach to reduce harm, why young children are more at risk, and sources and exposure-reduction methods for two of asbestos, radon and mold.
solution:
(a)(i) Two pollutants: carbon monoxide, particulate matter (also NOₓ, SOₓ, VOCs). *(2.)* (ii) Illness: particulates are linked to asthma, bronchitis, COPD or lung cancer; CO causes poisoning. *(1.)*

(b) Approach: install a chimney or ventilation, or switch to a cleaner-burning stove or fuel. Why it works: pollutants are vented out or less is produced, so indoor exposure and respiratory illness fall. *(1 + 1.)*

(c) Young children breathe more air per kilogram of body mass, have developing lungs and immune systems and narrower airways, and spend more time indoors. *(1 for one reason.)*

(d) Pick two. Asbestos: source is old insulation, tiles or building materials; reduce exposure by sealing or leaving undisturbed, or professional removal. Radon: source is uranium-bearing rock and soil seeping through the foundation; reduce by sealing cracks and installing a sub-slab vent. Mold: source is damp or flooded areas; reduce by repairing leaks, ventilating or dehumidifying and cleaning. *(1 per source, 1 per method; 4.)*
